14-095.r: Wrong pair: minorities' educational institutions → Article 30, not 31. Article 31 (property acquisition) repealed by 44th Amendment 1978; property now a legal right, Article 300-A.

14-096.r: Article 30 → minorities' right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 29 → protection of minorities' interests; 26 → manage religious affairs.

14-098.r: Article 30 does not define 'minorities'; Constitution recognises only religious and linguistic minorities. Both true, but R does not explain A.

14-099.r: Constitution recognises religious and linguistic minorities (not ethnic). Article 29 → conserve distinct language, script, culture; Article 30 → minorities' educational institutions.

14-100.r: Fundamental Rights enforced by the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226); Article 13 gives them judicial review to void laws violating them.

14-101.r: Guardian of Fundamental Rights → Judiciary (Supreme Court under Article 32, High Courts under Article 226).

14-104.r: Supreme Court → protector of citizens' Fundamental Rights and Guardian of the Constitution: enforces rights via Article 32 and interprets the Constitution.

14-105.r: Guardian of Fundamental Rights is the Judiciary, not the President. True: K.M. Munshi was in the Drafting Committee; Balwant Rai Mehta Committee 1957 recommended Panchayati Raj.

14-106.r: Article 32 enforces only Fundamental Rights (Part III) through writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari.

14-107.r: Article 32 → 'heart and soul' of the Constitution (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar): lets a person directly approach the Supreme Court when Fundamental Rights are violated.

14-108.r: Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) → 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution' per Dr. B.R. Ambedkar; without it the Constitution would be a nullity.
14-108.h: 32 teeth guard the mouth; Article 32 guards all Fundamental Rights.
hi: Right to Constitutional Remedies (संवैधानिक उपचारों का अधिकार)

14-109.r: Both true, R explains A: Ambedkar called Article 32 the very soul of the Constitution because it gives an effective remedy against violation of Fundamental Rights.

14-110.r: Article 32(2) → SC issues Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari; Article 32(3) → Parliament may by law empower any other court with these powers.

14-111.r: Article 32 → Supreme Court issues five writs for Fundamental Rights; Article 226 → High Court issues them for Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose'.
14-111.t: High Court writ power (Article 226) is wider than the Supreme Court's (Article 32).

14-112.r: Habeas Corpus → greatest safeguard of personal liberty: detainer must produce the detained person before court; freed if detention has no legal justification.

14-113.r: High Court (Article 226) secures individual liberty through Habeas Corpus → release of a person detained illegally.

14-114.r: Habeas Corpus = 'to have the body of': court has the detained person brought before it to check the grounds of detention → protects personal liberty.

14-115.r: Habeas Corpus → let us have the body; Mandamus → we command; Prohibition → writ to subordinate courts; Certiorari → be more fully informed; Quo-Warranto → by which authority.

14-116.r: Wrong pair: 'To be certified' → Certiorari, not Prohibition. Certiorari: higher court takes over a pending case from a lower court or quashes its order.

14-117.r: 'Postmortem' writ → Certiorari (higher courts re-examine subordinate court decisions); Quo warranto (checks a claim to public office) also has a postmortem sense.
14-117.c: The book prints (c), BPSC's key, but its explanation argues for (e) since Quo warranto also fits. Certiorari, which quashes an order already passed, is the writ usually called 'postmortem'.

14-118.r: Mandamus ('we command') → superior court orders a lower court, government officer or institution to perform its duty.

14-120.r: Wrong pair: Articles 23-24 = Right against Exploitation, not Freedom of Religion (25-28). Equality 14-18; Freedom 19-22; Cultural and Educational 29-30.
14-120.h: Block sizes five-four-two-four-two: Equality, Freedom, Exploitation, Religion, Cultural-Educational.

14-121.r: Cultural and Educational Rights → Articles 29-30; Constitutional Remedies → Article 32; Right against Exploitation → Articles 23-24; Right to Equality → Articles 14-18.

14-122.r: 16(2) → no discrimination in public appointment; 29(2) → no denial of admission to State-aided institutions; 30(1) → minorities' educational institutions; 31(1) → property deprived only by law.

14-123.r: Wrong pair: protection against arrest and detention → Article 22, not 23. Correct: untouchability 17, freedom of religion 25, minorities' interests 29.

14-124.r: Abolition of Titles → Article 18; Freedom to manage religious affairs → Article 26; Protection of language of minorities → Article 29; Right to Education → Article 21-A.

14-125.r: Fundamental Duties → 42nd Amendment; Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights → Keshvanand Bharti case; Basic Structure → Minerva Mills case (per this key); trafficking ban → Article 23.
14-125.t: Basic Structure was first propounded in Kesavananda Bharati and affirmed in Minerva Mills; this key pairs it with Minerva Mills.

14-126.r: Incorrect: Right to Die is not a Fundamental Right; Constitution is quasi-federal, not fully federal; FRs can be amended, not removed. Correct: Part III resembles US Bill of Rights.

14-127.r: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) → in a conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles (case on community-based medical college seat reservation).

14-128.r: Keshvananda Bharati (1973) → Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights. Earlier: Shankari Prasad 1951, Sajjan Singh 1965 allowed it; Golaknath 1967 denied it.

14-129.r: Chronology: Shankari Prasad (1951) → Sajjan Singh (1965) → Golaknath (1967, reversed both) → Kesavananda Bharati.
14-129.h: S-S-G-K: Shankari, Sajjan, Golaknath, Kesavananda, in alphabet-like march.

14-130.r: Doctrine of Basic Structure → Keshvananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), majority judgment; approved in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980).

14-132.r: Chronology: A.K. Gopalan (1950) → Golaknath (1967) → Keshvananda Bharati (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980).

14-133.r: Right to Property → removed as a Fundamental Right by 44th Amendment Act 1978; now Article 300-A, a legal right available to any person (not citizens only).

14-135.r: Right to Property is now a legal (statutory) right, not a Fundamental Right; the book accepts both 'Statutory Right' and 'Legal Right'.

14-138.r: Right to Property: legal right, not Fundamental. Article 301 = freedom of trade, commerce, intercourse. 44th Amendment 1978 (Janta Party Government) omitted 19(1)(f), inserted Article 300-A.

14-143.r: Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights → 44th (Forty-fourth) Constitutional Amendment; now a legal right.

14-148.r: The six Fundamental Rights do not include a 'Right to protest'; Equality, against Exploitation and Freedom of Religion are included.

14-149.r: Constitution grants Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Freedom (19-22), Freedom of Religion (25-28); there is no 'Right of Equal Shelter'.

14-150.r: Right to Information is not expressly in the Constitution; the Supreme Court reads it into freedom of speech and expression, Article 19(1)(a).

14-151.r: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala: no one can be compelled to sing the National Anthem; forcing it violates Articles 19(1)(a) and 25(1); no law obliges singing.

14-152.r: Citizens only, not aliens: freedom of speech and expression (Article 19) and minorities' cultural-educational rights (Article 29). Equality before law and life-liberty are for all.

14-154.r: Freedom of expression (Article 19) is citizens-only. Also for foreigners: equality before law (Article 14), Articles 20, 21, 21-A, right against exploitation, freedom of religion.

14-155.r: Equal protection of laws (Article 14) → all persons; right against discrimination, speech (19(1)(a)) and cultural-educational rights (29-30) → citizens only.

14-156.r: Equality before law (Article 14) → every person. Citizens only: right against discrimination, free movement (19(1)(d)), right to contest elections.

14-157.r: Right to Constitutional Remedies → for citizens and non-citizens; freedom of speech, free movement and acquiring property → citizens only.

14-158.r: A British citizen in India cannot claim freedom of trade and profession (Article 19(1)(g), citizens only); can claim equality before law, life and liberty, religious freedom.

14-159.r: Citizens-only rights: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30; so a British citizen in India lacks freedom of trade and profession (Article 19).

14-161.r: National minority status → can run own educational institutions and benefit from PM's 15-Point Programme; no automatic Lok Sabha nomination by the President.

14-162.r: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 replaced the Ordinance of 25 October 1975; Article 23(1) bans traffic in human beings and forced labour.
